clue.text: Permitted king's observers on the road

definitions.text: Permitted king's observers on the road

blocks.note: surface: officials allowed to watch over a monarch

blocks.clueFragment: Permitted king's observers on the road
blocks.note: setter's reading: the proverb says a cat may look at a king, so its eyes are licensed royal watchers, set into the road

explanation.surface: Royal watchers, given leave, keep an eye on the highway like licensed spies.
explanation.walkthrough: The proverb 'a cat may look at a king' makes a cat's gaze the permitted one. Cat's-eyes are the reflecting studs set along a road's centre line.
explanation.definitionFit: Reflective road studs are named after feline pupils glinting in headlights, and the proverb grants felines leave to stare at monarchs.

clue.text: The shrewdest copper on trial?

blocks.note: Cu is the chemical symbol for copper
a trial is a test

explanation.surface: The cleverest policeman finds himself in the dock.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Copper' looks like a police officer but is the metal; in a down clue 'on' puts it above the next piece.
explanation.definitionFit: Cute in its older sense means sharp-witted or clever, so the superlative is shrewdest.

clue.text: Bin the rat upset in parson's corn store

indicators.note: upset means knocked over and disordered, so the words before it are jumbled

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A rat knocks a bin over in the vicar's granary.
explanation.definitionFit: Parishioners once paid a tenth of their produce to the clergy, stored in a large barn kept for that purpose.

clue.text: The family diamonds went with the title?

definitions.text: The family diamonds went with the title

blocks.clueFragment: The family diamonds went with the title
blocks.note: surface: heirloom jewels passed down along with an inherited rank
setter's reading: the name in the title of a Trollope novel about a family's diamonds

explanation.walkthrough: Trollope's novel The Eustace Diamonds turns on whether a necklace was a family heirloom; 'title' means the book's title, not a peerage.
explanation.definitionFit: Trollope named his novel after the family whose diamonds are disputed, so their surname goes with them in the title.

clue.text: Sinner right away goes up to Clare's place

indicators.note: away means sent off, so a letter is taken out of the word before
in a down clue going up means reading from the bottom upwards

blocks.note: taken as written
R is the abbreviation for right

explanation.surface: A sinner rises to heaven to join a woman called Clare.
explanation.walkthrough: Clare is an Irish county, not a woman; Ennis is its county town.
explanation.definitionFit: Ennis is the county town of County Clare in the west of Ireland.

clue.text: 23 may get so drastically punished · (like 24)

blocks.note: first meaning: a heavy drinker may end up very drunk
second meaning: pelted with rocks as an execution
third meaning: fruit with the kernels taken out

explanation.walkthrough: Three meanings of one word: 23 is TIPPLER, who may get very drunk; 24 is PLUMS, fruit that can have their pits removed.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means heavily intoxicated, executed by pelting with rocks, and having had the pits removed, as fruit often is.

clue.text: Crusader can't change colour bar to progress

indicators.note: to change something is to alter it, so the letters of the word before are rearranged

blocks.note: letters taken without the apostrophe
the colour of a stop light, which bars traffic from moving on

explanation.surface: A crusading knight cannot alter the colour bar standing in the way of progress.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Colour bar' looks like racial discrimination; it is the colour that stops traffic. Tancred was a Norman leader of the First Crusade.
explanation.definitionFit: Tancred of Hauteville was a Norman knight and a leading commander in the First Crusade.

clue.text: 6's rough interior shell

indicators.note: the interior of a word is what is left inside once its ends are dropped
rough means untidy and unformed, so the kept letters are muddled

blocks.note: 6 is the Crusader answer, used without its first and last letters

explanation.surface: A crusader's rough inner shell, as if beneath his armour.
explanation.definitionFit: Nacre is mother-of-pearl, the iridescent material lining a mollusc's shell, so it stands for shell.

clue.text: Reveal what causes a record to go too slowly ?

blocks.note: a gramophone record is a disc
a clock that runs slow is said to lose

explanation.surface: Someone asks what makes a record player run slow.
explanation.definitionFit: To disclose is to make known something hidden, the same as revealing it.

clue.text: Handcuff couple on obstruction in court

blocks.note: a brace is a pair, as of game birds
a let is an obstruction in tennis or old law, and the court is a tennis court

explanation.surface: A pair are handcuffed for obstructing justice in the courtroom.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Court' suggests a law court, but it is a tennis court, where a let is a serve obstructed by the net.
explanation.definitionFit: Bracelets is old police slang for handcuffs, the metal rings locked round a prisoner's wrists.

clue.text: Roman general reissued road units with tunics

indicators.note: something reissued comes out again in a new form, so these letters are put out in a fresh order

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: An army re-equips its road units, handing out fresh tunics.
explanation.walkthrough: The general is the title character of Shakespeare's bloodiest Roman tragedy.
explanation.definitionFit: Shakespeare's tragedy centres on a victorious military commander returning to ancient Rome from wars against the Goths.

clue.text: The bishop's home truths for the playground?

definitions.note: a description of the answer's place rather than a noun synonym

blocks.note: a bishop's see is his diocese or seat; the 's doubles as 'is', joining this to what follows
a saw is an old saying, a proverbial truth

explanation.surface: Some home truths delivered at the bishop's residence, apparently fit for children.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The bishop's home' is SEE with the 's read as 'is'; saws are proverbs.
explanation.definitionFit: Seesaws are pivoting planks that children ride up and down in parks and school play areas.

clue.text: Type of lens clear on adjustment

definitions.note: the answer is an adjective naming that type

indicators.note: an adjustment rearranges things, so the letters before it are reset into new order

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: An optician says a lens becomes clear once it has been adjusted.
explanation.definitionFit: A corneal lens is a contact lens that sits on the clear front surface of the eyeball.

clue.text: Flower's warning of a fabulous racer's approach?

definitions.text: warning of a fabulous racer's approach

blocks.note: first meaning: a wild plant with blue bell-shaped blooms

blocks.clueFragment: warning of a fabulous racer's approach
blocks.note: second meaning: a bell rung to announce the fast animal from Aesop's fable racing the tortoise

explanation.walkthrough: 'Fabulous' means from a fable: the racer is the animal beaten by the tortoise, and a bell would warn of its coming.
explanation.definitionFit: The harebell is a slender wild bluebell of heaths and grassland, and split up the word names a warning chime for a hare.

clue.text: Heavens! Men repay strangely

indicators.note: done strangely means done in an odd way, so the letters come out in an odd order

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: An exclamation of surprise that some men are paying back what they owe in an odd way.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Heavens!' reads as an exclamation, but it is the noun for the sky.
explanation.definitionFit: The empyrean is the highest heaven or the sky above, in classical and poetic usage.

clue.text: Fists, the natural exponents of the noble art

definitions.text: the natural exponents of the noble art

blocks.note: first meaning: slang for the hands raised to fight

blocks.clueFragment: the natural exponents of the noble art
blocks.note: second meaning: peers of the realm, who would naturally practise anything called noble

explanation.walkthrough: The noble art is boxing; the joke is that the highest-ranking nobles should be its natural practitioners.
explanation.definitionFit: 'Put up your dukes' is slang for raising clenched hands, and dukes are also top-ranking aristocrats.

clue.text: Supporters given jobs by royal appointment?

blocks.note: first meaning: upright timbers that hold up a roof ridge
second meaning: positions filled by a monarch

explanation.walkthrough: 'Supporters' looks like fans or loyalists; it is structural timbers. Split, the word is posts in a monarch's gift.
explanation.definitionFit: These vertical beams run from a tie-beam to a roof's apex to brace it, and split they are posts a monarch appoints to.

clue.text: Confused excitement taking housing in rotation

blocks.note: a flat is a dwelling
spin is rotation

explanation.surface: Someone is in a whirl after getting a home through a rota scheme.
explanation.definitionFit: Being in a flat spin is a British idiom for a state of agitated panic and confusion.

clue.text: Engineer has nothing for reversing the ship

indicators.note: the combined pieces are run backwards before they make the answer

blocks.note: the Royal Engineers, a British army corps
nil means nothing

explanation.surface: A ship's engineer has nothing to do with putting the vessel astern.
explanation.definitionFit: An ocean liner is a large passenger ship running on a regular route.

clue.text: Save from investment

blocks.note: surface: put money aside out of what one has invested
setter's reading: investment is the military word for a siege, and a besieged town is rescued

explanation.walkthrough: Investment is not finance here: to invest a town is to besiege it, and an army that lifts the siege rescues the town.
explanation.definitionFit: To relieve a besieged town is to break the encirclement and rescue its defenders.

clue.text: Shoot the works—like Isabella's Basil

definitions.note: the definition describes the answer by example

blocks.note: to pot is to take a shot at game
a plant is a factory or works

explanation.surface: Fire at the whole factory, just as in a Keats poem.
explanation.walkthrough: In Keats's poem 'Isabella, or the Pot of Basil', she buries her lover's head in a pot of basil.
explanation.definitionFit: Isabella grew her basil in a pot, so it was an indoor potted specimen of exactly this sort.

clue.text: Not yet a pupil on the side

blocks.note: not now but later
taken as written
L for a learner, as on a British learner driver's plate

explanation.surface: A pupil not yet ready is left on the sidelines.
explanation.definitionFit: Lateral describes something situated at or towards the side, as a sideways position.

clue.text: Turning point for King Charles on the river

blocks.note: Carolus Rex, the Latin royal cipher
the name of the Thames as it flows through Oxford

explanation.surface: A decisive moment for Charles I when he reached the Thames.
explanation.walkthrough: CR is Carolus Rex, Charles the King; the Isis is the Thames at Oxford, where Charles I kept his wartime court.
explanation.definitionFit: A crisis is the decisive moment when events take a turn for better or worse.

clue.text: One who gives about a pound in the boozer

indicators.note: about means going round, so one word is wrapped around another

blocks.note: someone who gives a gratuity
L is the abbreviation for a pound sterling

explanation.surface: A generous customer tips the barman about a pound in the pub.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Boozer' reads as a pub in the surface, but here it is the person who drinks.
explanation.definitionFit: A habitual drinker of alcohol is called both a boozer and a tippler.

clue.text: Jobs for the boys, such as Horner ?

blocks.note: first meaning: choice positions handed to favoured insiders
second meaning: fruit like the one Little Jack Horner pulled out with his thumb

explanation.walkthrough: Little Jack Horner, of the nursery rhyme, put in his thumb and pulled out a plum.
explanation.definitionFit: Plum jobs are the most desirable posts, often given to cronies, and the rhyme's boy pulled one such fruit from his pie.

clue.text: Does one leave this violent man to cool his heels!

definitions.text: Does one leave this violent man to cool his heels

blocks.clueFragment: Does one leave this violent man to cool his heels
blocks.note: surface: is a hothead left waiting to calm down?
setter's reading: a rider's heel carries a spike that would need cooling if it were hot

explanation.surface: Someone wonders whether to leave a hothead waiting until he calms down.
explanation.walkthrough: Harry Percy, the rash rebel of Shakespeare's Henry IV, was nicknamed for his impetuous temper; split, his name is a heated spike on a heel.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means a rash, impetuous person, and was the nickname of the fiery Harry Percy.

clue.text: Would he add up to an Ibsen character?

indicators.note: in a down clue going up means the word is read from the bottom upwards

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Would this man amount to a character from a Norwegian play?
explanation.walkthrough: 'Add up to' looks like 'amount to'; 'up' instead turns the second word round.
explanation.definitionFit: Hedda Gabler is the title heroine of Ibsen's 1891 play.

clue.text: Lipped set for fruit, with colourful glasses

blocks.note: dried plums
with means and
glass prisms split light into colours

explanation.surface: A pout prepared for some fruit and coloured glassware.
explanation.walkthrough: In Dickens's Little Dorrit, Mrs General has young ladies say 'prunes and prisms' to shape their lips into a prim, genteel expression.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase was recited to set the mouth into a prim pursed shape, so it names a lip arrangement.

clue.text: Vulgar "eats" for a stag party?

blocks.note: surface: rough food laid on for a groom's night out
setter's reading: one who eats, in slang, and also something for a party with no woman, split as NO SHE plus R

explanation.surface: Crude food is laid on for a groom's all-male night out.
explanation.walkthrough: Nosh is slang for food or eating, so a nosher is an eater; a stag party is a 'no she' affair.
explanation.definitionFit: Nosh is slangy food, and someone who noshes is an eater, so the word is the vulgar name for one.

clue.text: Motor records of Spanish legitimists

blocks.note: a motor is a car
lists are records

explanation.surface: Vehicle registration files kept on Spanish royalists.
explanation.definitionFit: Carlists backed Don Carlos and his heirs as the rightful line to the Spanish throne, so they were Spain's legitimist faction.
